title: Making Peace with Time 𓆣
excerpt: Learning to make peace with time is the way in which we can actually experience our love, in the form of presence.

blocks.text: "You are no longer moving through time. It's time moving through you."
From a dharma talk and class at Jivamukti Yoga Paris, autumn 2026

We've almost made it to the end of the week, and you can feel the energy. At this moment in the city, it's very intense. Maybe it's difficult to ground down. Maybe it's difficult to feel relaxed. It can even be challenging to sleep at night. So it's nice that we can use our āsana practice to reconnect with the ground beneath us and, more importantly, to reconnect with our presence, which neutralizes this experience of rushing through time.

This idea of neutralizing the experience of rushing is very powerful and very important, because so often we project ourselves through our minds into an idealized version of the future in order to escape what we cannot be present for in this moment right now. And we practice this almost constantly. Thinking about how much I would love to be on the beach somewhere, how much I would love to finally get to the weekend, how much I would love to be done with this project, how much I would love to finally move to another city. All the time we're projecting our mind into the future.

When we're flying, when we're on a long train ride or a long car ride, we're really ready to get there, no? So we're pushing our mind into the future. There's only three hours left. There's only two hours left. There's only an hour left. But when we practice that habitually, over and over again, this idea that we're trying to kill time, slowly, it's actually time that's killing us. So we have to learn how to make peace with time. Otherwise our minds will always be programmed to look for the next thing. When you finally do land, when you finally get to that beach, or that new home, or that weekend, or the end of the project, your habit is to think: what's next?

I know I have this habit. I inherited it from my mother, who I love very much. But we have a bad habit in our family. We plan a vacation for a long time. We're going to see each other for the first time in ten months. We're going to do this nice thing. And we get there, and on the first day of the vacation my mom says to me: "What should we do next? Where should we go next?" We're already pushing ourselves ahead to the next moment.

When we're trying to fast forward through our lives, it's only when we get to the end that we realize we skipped the really sweet part. We skipped the marrow, the nectar, the essence of what it means to be alive. Which means being here, even in the moments that are a little bit heavy, even in the moments that are not yet clear, even in the moments that require a little bit more intensity. And even in the moments, particularly in the moments, when nothing is required of us except a state of acceptance, a state of calm.

Learning to make peace with time is the way in which we can actually experience our love, which we've talked about so much over the last two weeks, in the form of presence. Love and presence, being the same thing, arise when we allow ourselves to be aligned, synchronized between body and mind, in the here and now. It's very easy to talk about the here and now, but all of you who have taken the time to sit down for meditation for five minutes know how far that is from the habit we hold. So we're retraining ourselves, through our āsana practice and our meditation practice, to come back, over and over again, to the only place we can ever experience love: the here and the now.

To make peace with time, we can even invoke the goddess of time herself. Perhaps sometimes we see her as very fierce. Sometimes she's called the all-devouring mother: Kālī. Her very name comes from kāla, time. The Mahānirvāṇa Tantra sings it this way: Mahākāla is the one who devours all beings at the dissolution of things, and "since Thou devourest Mahākāla Himself, it is Thou who art the Supreme Primordial Kālikā" (4.31). She is the one who swallows even time.

Many of us who have seen images of Mahākālī find that there's something to be afraid of. But in truth, when we align with this energy of Kālī through the mantra, we find the ability she holds to cut through all of that speed, all of that noise, and arrive back at the place that has always been here: this eternal center. Through making peace with time, we start to see a light and a life that exist beyond the confines of an imagined past and an imagined future.
Māmbā Lalitā Devī Mahākālī Bhairavī
"My mother, the playful goddess, great Kālī, the awe-inspiring one."

On the mat, this becomes very simple. Inhaling, experiencing presence here. Exhaling, letting go of all your worries that have to do with the past, and then anything that has to do with the future. You only have to live this breath, one breath at a time. You only have to live this life, one breath at a time. Not by being inactive, but by being actively present. Because the biggest tax on our energy is the noise of the mind, all that worry about past and future, and the breath cuts through it. The breath will help you more than thinking can.
And when you stop fast forwarding, you notice something. Thoughts and emotions flow through you. Nothing can contain this presence. This presence contains it all.

Mahākālī recycles the cells of the body through the process of death. We certainly don't carry the physical form with us. We don't even carry the memories in our minds. But what we carry forward into our next life is our desire. So if you don't want to repeat this pattern of waiting and frustration in this life, give yourself permission to experience the emotion that you desire. Drop out of this imagining, this evaluation of what came before, this projection of what might come next, and experience this ground: ever present, ever fresh, the fertile ground in which it's possible for love to arise. Here, you can work with what is to create the emotional state that you desire.

Thinking, now I have to do this, before that I already had to take care of that. The truth is, you're here. Everything arises here. If you want to feel joy, if you want to find love, the only place that you can feel or find it is here and now.

Find a comfortable seat. Feel yourself rooted. Feel yourself liberated from the fiction of what's coming next. This moment that you have never left is itself the Great Mother, and you are that: your awareness, the infinite space through which time is free to pass. Notice your tendency to try to get somewhere else, and let it go, just ever so slightly, as you exhale. Each time you exhale, let time, space, tension and thought flow through you without getting attached. Perhaps you're free to notice how love arises naturally when we let go of fear and return to our true form, that of formless presence.

Press your hands together in front of your heart, bringing space and time together before their source: this awareness, this heart, which eternally radiates and shines forth. Make an offering of any peace, any joy, any love you've had the chance to find, knowing that an offering is redoubled as this vibration passes through you.
Bow your head down toward your heart, in gratitude for this day, for this life.
Sources
Avalon, Arthur (Sir John Woodroffe), trans. Tantra of the Great Liberation (Mahānirvāṇa Tantra). London: Luzac & Co., 1913. Chapter 4, verses 30 to 32.

title: You Are Not Just a Body 𓄣
excerpt: Śiva Sūtra 1.19: the body arises from union with power. What is the mantra you're repeating all the time?

blocks.text: "What is the mantra that you're repeating all the time?"
From a dharma talk given at Jivamukti Yoga Paris, autumn 2026

Something rather alarming is happening. Many of us are not satisfied with the way our bodies are, how they look or the way we feel in them. This epidemic of dissatisfaction with our physical form stirs up a lot of frustration, fear, hatred and jealousy that ultimately doesn't help us on our spiritual path. And by spiritual path, I don't mean some path to an esoteric other world. I mean living well, living deeply, living beautifully in this world, in this body.

It's nobody's fault that we might feel dissatisfied with our bodies, because we're being bombarded every day with images of bodies that are unattainable. Women at forty years old are told to look like they have the body of someone who's sixteen, and guys are taught from the time they're seven years old that they should look like Superman or Goku. On top of that, we have endless images edited not only by Photoshop but by AI, to the point where we feel like we're not even qualified as human anymore. That we're just a shadow of the real thing.

And because of that, maybe we come to a yoga class and we think: great, I'm going to push myself, I'm going to come every day and I'm going to get an amazing shape. And then people will be attracted to me. People will care about me. People will love me. Why? Because my body is good enough. This belief that love comes through the way that we appear physically in the world is one of the greater illusions we have to overcome.

The body, according to the yogis, is just something you wear, like a set of clothing, for a short period of time, be it forty or fifty or seventy-five years. Eventually, when the clothes have holes in them, without any worry, you throw them away and you take on a new set of garments. In the same vein, the yogi remains unattached to the way the body naturally changes over time. So we grow old. So we get wrinkles. So maybe we put on a little bit of belly fat. So what? This is just the way a human body progresses through time.

Our bodies are changing all the time. They're changing with the seasons. So take it as no surprise: over the next three months, now that we've entered autumn, as it gets colder, you'll want to eat more. And then one day you'll say, oh my God, I don't look as in shape as I did this summer. Don't panic.

The body itself, according to the ancient teachings, doesn't arise out of a lot of frustration and a lot of fear. It arises out of power. Today's mantra comes from the Śiva Sūtras, first chapter, nineteenth sūtra. The sūtras were revealed to the sage Vasugupta in Kashmir in the early ninth century, some twelve hundred years ago. Tradition says Śiva showed these verses to him in dream, and later he found them inscribed on a rock. Not written, but received.
Śakti-sandhāne śarīrotpattiḥ

Śakti means energy, power: the supreme power, the source. Sandhāne means joining with, unifying with, from sam, meaning equal or together. Śarīra is the body. Utpattiḥ means arising, the creation of. So: through unifying with Śakti, there is the creation of the body.
Kṣemarāja, the great eleventh-century tantric scholar and practitioner, commented on this verse in his Śiva Sūtra Vimarśinī:
yadānusandhatte dārḍhyena tanmayībhavati, tadā tadvaśenāsya yathābhimataṁ śarīram utpadyate
"When he unites with that power and becomes firmly absorbed in it, then, through its force, a body arises for him as he wills."

He said that when the yogi is connected with this pure power, this pure source, they can manifest any body that they like. And for Kṣemarāja, śarīra isn't only this physical body. It is any form the yogi's empowered will brings forth: a body, an object, a whole world:
yathecchābhyarthito dhātā jāgrato'rthān hṛdi sthitān / somasūryodayaṁ kṛtvā sampādayati dehinaḥ
"Just as, when entreated by desire, the Creator brings forth for the waking one the aims held in his heart…"

Why? Because this universe that seems solid, that seems material, is in itself only vibration. It is made up of the desires, the imaginatings, the intentions, the words, and of course the actions that we give as input into this life.

We think the body is something very solid, very stable, very physical. But when we change the vibration coming from our core, the body naturally starts to realign with that vibration. So ask yourself: what is the mantra that you're repeating all the time? I hate myself. I'm not good enough. I'm not beautiful. I'm not worthy. In some form or another, billions of people on Earth today are repeating that mantra.

And when we go into the yoga practice, or any other physical activity, with stress, frustration, fear, doubt and a sense of jealous competition, we start to manifest that as our physical body. Over time, we have a body that's exhausted rather than enlivened by what it does in the world. And this isn't only yogic poetry. Researchers who followed more than ten thousand men and women for nearly twenty years found that chronic stress predicted weight gathering around the waist, and the stress hormone cortisol helps explain why: it tells the body to store fat around the belly, and it quiets the thyroid, the gland that sets the pace of our metabolism. The way we meet the world can literally shape the body we live in. You can practice and practice until you feel that you have unlimited energy and an unlimited life. But that practice has to be enlivened with a mantra that's full of joy.

So start by repeating a mantra from your center that is made out of love. You could repeat Oṃ Namaḥ Śivāya. You could repeat Māmbā Lalitā Devī Parāśakti Sundarī. Or you could even start in English, or in French: je m'aime, je m'aime, je m'aime. Whatever aligns with the experience of love for your core.

Overcoming all the noise from the world requires you to cut through with the sword of the breath. With each exhalation, you can cut through the noise, not pushing it away, not arguing with it, but merging breath with mantra. That's the sword. It's as simple as this: inhale, repeat the mantra in your mind. Exhale, repeat the mantra in your mind. Try it during practice today. As you notice noise coming up in the mind, cut through over and again.

The way I understand the tantrikas: if you want to change the world, first prove to yourself you can manifest the body that you desire, and then you'll start to be able to bring forth a wider reality around you. It isn't like now I've manifested a nice six-pack and a nice ass, and I'm happy just chilling while the world is suffering. It's learning this power of creation through the ability to harness and incarnate your imagination. Many of us can imagine how we're not good enough. It's easy for us to imagine that things will only ever go badly, that one day we won't be loved, that one day we'll be forgotten, that one day we will all just blow up. How much more powerful it is to imagine the life and the world that you deeply desire.

This capitalist world has given you every framework to detest yourself, to distrust yourself, to think that when you're finally good enough, because you have a nicer body or a nicer car or a bigger house, then and only then will people love you and accept you. The truth is, love is who you are, and you can align with who you are by dropping the illusion that you are just a body. You are something far more: a pure vibration, a pure radiation coming from the center, coming from the source. Relaxing into that is perhaps the highest form of revolution, or at least the most realistic revolution we can create through our own efforts today.
So let's chant this mantra together. Taking a deep breath in.
Śakti-sandhāne śarīrotpattiḥ
This body is manifesting anew through the mantra you're repeating in your mind.

Draw your hands together in front of your heart center. Before you give it any thought, allow the mantra to bring forth there that which you most deeply desire, that beauty that you naturally cherish. Allow it to rest like a seed, rooted deeply there, now blossoming out into the light, like a flower opening to the sky. Allow this body to manifest in the higher way, in the spiritual way, aligned with the pure pulsation of life.

The continuation is to offer out whatever love, peace, tranquility and joy you found inside. Offer that to someone you love, so it grows deeper as it radiates out to all of your cells and beyond from your center. And perhaps you can go so far as to offer that to all beings, knowing that this is both our shared essence and our shared goal.
Sources
Vasugupta, Śiva Sūtras 1.19, śakti-sandhāne śarīrotpattiḥ.
Kṣemarāja, Śiva Sūtra Vimarśinī 1.19 (Sanskrit quoted; translation by the author). On śarīra as body, thought, breath and void, see his commentary on 1.14.
Spanda Kārikā 3.1, as cited by Kṣemarāja in his commentary on 1.19 (translation by the author).
Jaideva Singh, Śiva Sūtras: The Yoga of Supreme Identity (Motilal Banarsidass, 1979), recommended English translation.

Brunner, E. J., Chandola, T., & Marmot, M. G. (2007). "Prospective effect of job strain on general and central obesity in the Whitehall II Study." American Journal of Epidemiology, 165(7), 828–837. doi:10.1093/aje/kwk058
Tsigos, C., & Chrousos, G. P. (2002). "Hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal axis, neuroendocrine factors and stress." Journal of Psychosomatic Research, 53(4), 865–871. doi:10.1016/S0022-3999(02)00429-4

title: Ānanda and the Obstacle 𓄣
excerpt: Part three of a three-part series on love. Bliss has no opposite. Obstacles are invitations to remember.

blocks.text: Part three of a three-part series on love.
This is a dharma talk transcript from Sept 21, 2026.
The yogis tell us love is who we are. But hearing that confuses us slightly, because so often we experience emotions we'd consider the opposite of love.

According to the yogis, this state of ānanda, which is not a state, this experience of love, which is not an experience, doesn't have an opposite. It's not that there's love on one end and hate on the other. Love is the ground of our being. It is the rasa, the flavor, of our being. The Taittirīya Upaniṣad (2.7) says it simply: raso vai saḥ, "that is rasa," and whoever tastes it becomes blissful.

But what happens is like clouds in the sky. To our eyes, it can seem as if there's no sun up there. Of course, the sun is as present as ever. Something in our perception is blocking the recognition of what is eternally there, eternally constant, eternally present: this stateless state of love.
So what blocks that experience of love? We put conditions onto the unconditional. We're not doing this consciously. It's happening subconsciously, all the time.
I'd love to get to work on time, but as I'm biking, a little kid and his father are taking up the whole bike lane and going really slow. Whoa, where did my love go?
I'd love to have a peaceful morning doing yoga, totally tranquil, and then there's construction going on outside. Whoa, where did my love go?
I want to feel competent and confident, and in yoga class the teacher asks me to do something I'm pretty sure is impossible. Oh, where did my love go?

"I would love this, but then there's that." All of a sudden we find obstacles in our path, and we think they are a problem big enough to reduce our experience of bliss, or to cut off our connection to the light.

We have to remember that obstacles themselves are invitations to remember, invitations to grow. We might think that failure means we're a failure. But love is both the path and the goal. Every failure, seen from love, is love finding its way back to itself. In the Trika of Abhinavagupta, the means and the goal are finally not two.

That only happens when we let the conditional argument of the mind go: I would love this, but this person's in my way. I would love that, but the situation's all wrong. No. Love simply is, and we realize it is occurring when we relax out of the mind.

My dear friend and colleague Ian and I, who have taught together at the studio for six years, are well acquainted with obstacles and good reasons to feel frustrated. We're leading a retreat in Nepal, where tragic ecological circumstances have created obstacles for people all over the country, and certainly for us as hosts. But through those obstacles, we've found new ways to express our love, new solutions that arose from giving space to what's there. The people of Nepal contributed the least to climate change and are receiving the brunt of its effects, so as a gesture we're giving 10% of the retreat's profits to relief efforts there.

This is why we chant to Gaṇeśa, the placer and the remover of obstacles, Vighnakartā and Vighnahartā. You could call him the patron deity of love, of bliss, of the playfulness that naturally arises when we don't meet every situation with the baggage of our conditioned mind. The obstacle and its removal come from the same blissful one. The obstacle isn't a detour on the way to love. It is love's own play.
Oṃ Gaṃ Gaṇapataye Namaḥ

Join your hands together in front of your heart, and feel yourself taking refuge in the loving one, the blissful one, Gaṇeśa. His bliss and love are so free of any condition that, as the Purāṇas teach, even after his head was cut off by his father, all he could feel for Śiva was a deep love, a deep joy, and a deep laugh.
Knowing we are something far greater than the thoughts in our minds, take a deep breath.

title: The Ocean of Love 𓄣
excerpt: Part two of a three-part series on love. Love as the force that bridges every duality, and the ocean you already are.

blocks.text: Part two of a three-part series on love.
This is a dharma talk transcript from Sept 20, 2026.

Let's deepen our understanding of, or better yet our experience of, this very mysterious word called love. We throw it around all the time: I love pizza, I love my cat, I love you. But it's very difficult for us to understand the immensity of the force that is love itself.

Maybe the first thing that comes to mind is attraction between the masculine and the feminine. But love works as a force that transcends polarities. It doesn't matter if you're a man or a woman, with a man or with a woman, or anything in between. There's a pull between what seem like opposites. This is the mysterious power of love: it bridges the gap between seeming pairs of opposites.

There is also the deep love between parent and child, or grandparent and grandchild, that transcends the gap of young and old. There is a love that exists in the past and a love that exists in the future, and that love is the reason we all exist in the present. Some force of desire, some pull toward connecting beyond one's own individual boundaries, came together to create something more.
Love also transcends the boundary between internal and external. When we love someone, our circle of concern expands beyond our own body and mind.

And most profoundly, love transcends the duality of consciousness and energy. We experience this awareness in here and this world full of energy out there. According to the teachings of Tantra, love is the binding force between consciousness and experience, Śiva and Śakti. Love can transcend every concept of duality we place onto our lives. It's here all the time, regardless of the state we're in, concentrated or distracted.

But when we try to grab it, it's just like water. It slides right through our hands. How many of us have felt, "This is the one. I know she's right, he's right for me," and tried to grab it, and before we knew it, poof, they were gone?
Maybe this has only happened to me.

Love has a way of finding us when we learn how to relax. It's like what's always said about a butterfly. The more you chase it, the less likely it is to come and stay with you. But if you can relax and be calm, it might just come and alight on your shoulder for a little while.

Love is like that, but even more so. Love is the ocean of our awareness, the ocean of our existence that we inhabit all the time. You can swing your hands around in the water as much as you like. The water slides through your fingers, but you are never without this immersion in love.

Even saying we are in the ocean keeps a duality between inner and outer. Better said: we are the ocean of consciousness, the ocean of light, the ocean of love, embodying this wave-like form called "me" for a short period of time. As the wave rises and the wave crashes, for the ocean there's no drama at all. It's just the passing expression of its love for creation, for play, for dynamism.

So our practice is to allow ourselves to relax into who we are. Trying to be somebody all the time, well, it's a lot of work. And when we finally get exhausted of that, we can allow ourselves to be who we truly are, beyond the concepts and categories that are fundamentally dualistic, coming from the mind. We can allow ourselves to be the oneness, the source.
The mantra we chant is the expression of this recognition:

Sacarācara-paripūrṇaṃ śivo'ham

Cidānanda-svarūpaḥ śivo'ham

I am Śiva, filling all that moves and all that does not move. I am Śiva, whose very nature is consciousness and bliss." The refrain echoes Śaṅkara's Nirvāṇa Ṣaṭkam.

The mantra doesn't depend on being understood. Its sounds are Śakti itself, and they work whether or not the mind follows. But the Śiva Sūtras (2.1) teach cittaṃ mantraḥ, "awareness is mantra," and Kṣemarāja reads mantra through manana, contemplation: the reciter recognizing their identity with what is recited. The translation can't contain the ocean. It is a finger pointing to the ocean you already are.

Join your hands together in front of your heart. Bringing together these seeming opposites of left and right, we see that the two sides of the body are fundamentally one through the nexus of the heart.
Oṃ śānti.

title: Taking Refuge in the Heart 𓄣
excerpt: Part one of a three-part series on love. Yoga as learning to relax the mind into the heart, and to take refuge there.

blocks.text: Part one of a three-part series on love.
This is a dharma talk transcript from Sept 19, 2026.

When we practice together, we're in a relationship of trust. We're working together not only to go further in our physical practice, but to feel that we're supporting one another on the path of awakening. That means awakening to the meaning of a very mysterious yet often-used word: love. Most spiritual traditions, in one way or another, point toward the experience of love.

That word gets tangled up with our contemporary layer of concepts like dating, commitment, responsibility, and even ownership. These ideas don't necessarily refer back to the ancient idea of love, yet in many ways they rhyme with it. Wherever there is love, that love rests on the experience of trust. Trust is one of the main ingredients for the sensation of being loved and being able to love.

On the spiritual path, we learn to give ourselves the same trust we usually give to somebody else, and perhaps a much deeper trust. Trusting ourselves is not easy. Since we were very little, we've been given every indication that we need to be told to stay quiet, to follow the rules, to always be clean, to always attend to whatever we're told is important. We learn to trust the rules over our own inner signals. Over time, we start to abandon the idea that we're someone worthy of love, because we don't have a deep trust in who we are.

The path of yoga, in its shortest summation, could be described as learning how to relax your mind into your heart. In your heart there is an intuitive sense of kindness and compassion that doesn't know any bounds. It comes before any mental justification can come into play: "these people started it," or "somehow these people deserve it."

The moment we see images of war, of children dying for the causes of some man, or some group of people, hungry for power, our hearts immediately know that this is wrong. Our hearts can't bear to watch it. Then our minds jump in to protect our hearts: "Don't read the news too much. Don't look at that too closely. Somehow this is the way it has to be." But the heart doesn't need the protection of the mind. The mind needs the protection of the heart.

According to the great Tibetan yogis, the kindness and compassion in the heart, maitrī and karuṇā, are without limitation. With sympathetic joy and equanimity, they are counted among the four immeasurables. What we can start to do is trust the indications of our heart. Not mental explanation, but the feeling of being safe, or the feeling of being agitated and uneasy when we see something our hearts cannot fully bear to witness.

It's learning to trust that there is a goodness within us, a universal goodness that exists beyond mental creation. It doesn't need to be conditioned. It is naturally there. When we can trust and relax into our hearts, our responses to what is difficult and to what is beautiful, in our thoughts, our words, and our actions, will be much more deeply aligned with who we are.

Life is precious. Life is sacred. Life is something to be nurtured. And the experience of love is always enhanced when it's shared. The wisdom of the heart is the wisdom most necessary for our time, because it recognizes, without any force, that someone else's suffering is just as real as my own.
The mind is very good at making walls. The heart is very good at flooding the experience with deep understanding.

When we talk about nourishing, protecting, and honoring life, we often invoke Viṣṇu. In the Bhagavad Gītā (4.7–8), Kṛṣṇa says that whenever dharma declines, he takes form again, age after age, to restore it. Viṣṇu comes in his many avatars to restore balance: to bring love, the experience of the heart, back into the center.

The heart, not the brain, is the center of the spine. In the subtle body, anāhata, the heart center, sits at the middle of the seven cakras. The heart is the center of the column that is the manifestation of who you are. And the Gītā tells us who waits there. In 18.61, Kṛṣṇa says: īśvaraḥ sarva-bhūtānāṃ hṛd-deśe 'rjuna tiṣṭhati, "the Lord dwells in the heart of all beings, Arjuna." The one who comes to restore balance is already seated in your heart.
So there are many mantras we can use to relax into the heart. The one we're using this month is Vallabhācārya's eight-syllable mantra:
Śrī Kṛṣṇaḥ śaraṇaṃ mama Literally, "Śrī Kṛṣṇa is my refuge." Freely, and in light of the Gītā: "I take refuge in my heart."

Join your hands together in front of your heart, this space that offers the deep protection of wisdom and compassion, the refuge of light that exists beyond any temporary darkness we might experience in this life. Even beyond the momentary darkness of death, this heart light shines.

title: The Three Sisters 𓇳
excerpt: Icchā, jñāna, kriyā as will, knowledge, action. Pratibhā as the flash that makes understanding possible.

blocks.text: Icchā. Jñāna. Kriyā.
Kṣemarāja does not open the Pratyabhijñāhṛdayam with a technique. He opens with a fact:

चितिः स्वतन्त्रा विश्वसिद्धिहेतुः

citiḥ svatantrā viśva-siddhi-hetuḥ

The sovereign Śakti, absolute Consciousness, is the cause of the manifestation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe.

I am happy to be reading these layers in Pratibha. Citi is not your mood. It is the field in which a mood can appear. And that field is not inert. It wills. It knows. It does. In the Śaiva house these three powers are not optional extras of a finished God. They are the Goddess as she pulses. The tradition names them as sisters: icchā-śakti, jñāna-śakti, kriyā-śakti. Will. Knowledge. Action.
One pulse. Three faces.
If you have landed on Agni Agama before, you have already met them in English: Will it. Know it. Act it. This is that teaching elaborated from its source.
Most of us do not fail for lack of information. We fail because the three sisters have been divorced.

We want without knowing. We know without daring. We act without having first seen what we actually desire. The culture then sells us a counterfeit of each: want becomes algorithm, knowledge becomes opinion, action becomes grind. Paranoia is simply icchā turned against itself: imagination employed as a factory of threat. The nervous system is very good at this. It will staff an entire inner ministry of worst-case scenarios and call that realism.

Pronoia is not naïveté. It is icchā used as it was designed: the same imaginative power, pointed at what is deeply desired, assumed as already belonging to the possible. The universe does not owe you a plot. But consciousness is plot. It is, in Kṣemarāja's word, svatantrā: sovereign. To will consciously is to stop letting the unexamined image run the house.
Vasugupta is even shorter:

चैतन्यमात्मा

caitanyam ātmā

Consciousness is the Self.

The Siva Sutra does not instruct. It states what cannot be otherwise. If that is true, then the three sisters are not skills you acquire. They are how the Self already moves. Practice is only the courage to stop looking elsewhere.
Icchā: will what you deeply desire.

Icchā is not preference. Preference is the menu. Icchā is hunger that has recognized itself. In the body it feels like a lean, a heat, a refusal to go numb. The work is to make it conscious. Most desire is borrowed: family, market, the last person who frightened us. Conscious will asks a more intimate question: what do I actually want this life to taste like? Then it uses imagination as a ritual instrument. See it. Taste it. Let the image be specific enough that the nervous system has something true to organize around.

Pronoia begins here. Not "everything is fine." Rather: I will not spend my one wild faculty of seeing on catastrophe rehearsals. I will spend it on the form I am here to serve. If that sounds like magic, good. In this tradition, imagination is a śakti, not a hobby.
Jñāna: know where you are, and what is deeply beautiful.

Will without knowledge is fever. Jñāna is the sister who will not let you lie. Where are you, actually? What is the shape of this money, this body, this city, this love, this limitation? That refusal to blur has a name: viveka. Discrimination, not as coldness, but as the cut between the real and the borrowed, the shining and the merely shiny. Without viveka, jñāna collapses into opinion.

Beauty is not decoration. Beauty is the criterion. In Śaiva language, vimarśa is consciousness tasting itself. You know you are oriented when the thing you want is also the thing that, seen clearly, is beautiful. Not impressive, not brandable. Beautiful.

This is why the old texts refuse to separate metaphysics from aesthetics. To know the real is to find it shining. If your plan requires you to despise the ground you are standing on, it is not jñāna. It is escape wearing a strategy.
Kriyā: have the courage to act.

The third sister is the one Western spirituality most likes to skip, having confused stillness with virtue. Kriyā is the universe as verb. A will that never leaves the cushion is still paranoia: the image protected from contact. Action is how icchā tests whether it was true. You do not need a complete map. You need the next honest motion.
The Gītā has already said it, and it will say it again until we live it:

कर्मण्येवाधिकारस्ते मा फलेषु कदाचन।

karmaṇy evādhikāras te mā phaleṣu kadācana

Your authority is to the action alone, never to its fruits.
That is not quietism. That is kriyā stripped of the bargain. You act because the three sisters, together, have already moved. The fruit is not your department.
Other rivers say the same thing in other tongues. This is the point of Pratibha: not to flatten the traditions into one slogan, but to let them sit in one room until you hear the rhyme.

Epictetus, on the first page of the Enchiridion: some things are up to us, and some are not. The whole Stoic path is jñāna of that cut, then kriyā inside it. You can open it as a living passage in the library, not as a quote on a mug.

Heraclitus: ἦθος ἀνθρώπῳ δαίμων: a person's character is their daimon. Ethos is not costume. It is the shape your three sisters have taken in you. Change the will, the seeing, the deed, and you change the spirit that walks with you.
Lǎozǐ, in the Dào Dé Jīng: the journey of a thousand lǐ begins under the foot. Kriyā does not wait for the panorama. It honors the inch you can actually inhabit.

Ibn ʿArabī's line, which Pratibha keeps in the Know Yourself collection: who knows himself knows his Lord. Jñāna here is not information about a distant God. It is recognition. Pratyabhijñā. The flash.
That flash has a name. Pratibhā. Luminous intelligence. Not acquired learning, but the brilliance that makes understanding possible at all.

I built Pratibha as a living manuscript for exactly this work. Each passage is layered: original tongue, translation, commentary, key terms, cross-tradition resonances, a practice. You can read, sit with today's page, wander by random, walk a path, keep a journal, and ask the library to speak back in study chat without leaving the source.
The three sisters are not content to be admired. They want a room. Pratibha is one.

If icchā has been feeding paranoia, take a single image of what you deeply want and hold it until it warms. If jñāna has been floating, name where you actually are, and one thing that is already beautiful there. If kriyā has been waiting for permission, do the next small true thing before the day closes.
Will it. Know it. Act it.
The sisters are not coming. They are how you are already alive.
On the image

The three prongs are the sisters: icchā, jñāna, kriyā, rising from one lotus. At the crown, sauḥ, the heart-bīja of Parā in Trika, the Goddess as the whole sound. Oṃ hauṃ and hrīṃ oṃ are seed-sounds of Bhairava and of Śakti. In the blue lotus at the fork: oṃ namaḥ śivāya. Śivo'ham: I am Śiva. Hara hara mahādeva. Īśāna, the upward face. At the left foot, Tryambaka's mṛtyuñjaya, the prayer that loosens the bond of death. At the right, Paśupati, lord of the bound. The skulls are time. The lamps are the offering. The sisters are not three gods. They are one pulse, named three times.
Open Pratibha
What it is

title: A Crack in the Darkness 𓇳

blocks.text: “The present moment is the only moment available to us, and it is the door to all moments.”
THICH NHẤT HẠNH

The power of soulless inhumanity, which has always been a pervasive albeit masked force in our politics, is now on full display. Not Republican or Democrat, but psychopath. That is the Geist that inhabits now the White House, a love of death, the desire for a brief flash, the momentary vanishing of impotence the moment bombs fall.

We can no longer pretend the foundations are intact. Arms contracts and political debts are the forces that guide. The system requires endless war while healthcare, education, and feeding the poor have become preposterous propositions. More insane still: the religious fantasy on all sides, covenants that seem to prefer apocalypse over communication. We hold tight onto the worn-out blanket of these bedtime stories told by our ancestors, who had never imagined electricity, AI, climate change, or universal human rights. All this childish hubris. The chosen. The right. Anything rather than humbly admitting that we all wish to continue breathing.

The shock of what I see today glues my jaw to the floor. I listened well in Sunday School. There seemed to be a refrain when it came to the teachings of Christ: charity, forgiveness, love, and healing. How could any interpretation of love ever be more farcical than that which we see now masquerading in American flags?

It’s enough insanity to make a person want to say that everything is lost. And yet, how can we live, how can we resist? In the face of such a pernicious, illogical, and all-consuming beast, what tactics are most adaptive? Firstly, we must not rest complicit in our silence bought cheaply with comfort: endless sports spectacles or season twelve of another meaningless show, likes on socials for doing socially safe things while we scroll in climate-controlled rooms. What are all these worth when our minds reel and our hearts seethe with the injustice that we desperately try to ignore and avoid? Anesthetized in stimulation, until we don’t even respond when the missiles finally start to fly over our own heads. Resistance is medicine in a sick world.

And yet, secondly, we cannot out of guilt or crisis self-impose a cessation in the celebration of this miracle called life. Like Toi Derricotte said, “joy is resistance”. Each breath sings it, even if the mind feels hopelessly depressed as it muddles through media. In the face of ever-fresh hypocrisy and abomination, all of nature is buzzing with a desire for life. Nature dares even to mock the sadomasochistic human machine by singing its fecundity and ecstasy in every sunset and sunrise. Homeostasis, harmony, is spontaneously sought in every cell of every manifestation we call life. Because in truth, life loves life. Death might be necessary, might be revolutionary for evolutionary forces to perform, but worshiping death would be a deep misreading of the whole story. Like worshiping the last page of a chapter but not reading the ones that lead you there. Only a decapitated ego worships death. And yet this motherless child, who has forgotten he depends on the earth for life, works around the clock in Washington, in Tel Aviv, in Tehran worshipping the death of the “other” without recognizing he is inevitably conjuring his own destruction.

We must maintain our desire simultaneously to resist and to live well. Quiet comfort and existential regret are both tactics of the oppressor to win the war of soul capture. Numb you with entertainment or collapse you with guilt; either way you are removed from the field. First, you must recognize that the war is not only being waged out there but most fundamentally in you. But will you cave to its commands? Or will you carry on the work to celebrate this miracle called life? Even in the midst of the Holocaust, Viktor Frankl recounts: “Everything can be taken from a man but one thing: the last of the human freedoms — to choose one’s attitude in any given set of circumstances, to choose one’s own way. And there were always choices to make. Every day, every hour, offered the opportunity to make a decision, a decision which determined whether you would or would not submit to those powers which threatened to rob you of your very self, your inner freedom.”
—Man’s Search for Meaning (1946)

I believe we must maintain our effort to be in the world, and all the while to transcend it. Wise we would be to know our transcendental side. There is something in you, reading this now, that remains eternally unperturbed by the chaos and explosions around. There is a light that burns true in all this religious fanaticism. But the revelation is it doesn’t belong to any particular people, or nation, or tribe — it is the brilliance we are so completely blinded by we can only give cheap descriptions like ‘Life’.  We would do well to shore up our soul in that deep harbor. Lest we might lose ourselves in the same frenzy and fear as those who have obtained everything but have lost the Essential, and chronically feel the mania of never enough. Cleave to the light, for it is that which now is even illuminating the darkness we find.

Thomas Merton, the great Christian mystic, stated it plainly enough, that we must know peace to sow peace: “The rush and pressure of modern life are a form, perhaps the most common form, of… innate violence. To allow oneself to be carried away by a multitude of conflicting concerns, to surrender to too many demands, to commit oneself to too many projects, to want to help everyone in everything, is to succumb to violence. The frenzy of our activism neutralizes our work for peace. It destroys our own inner capacity for peace. It destroys the fruitfulness of our own work, because it kills the root of inner wisdom which makes work fruitful.” — Conjectures of a Guilty Bystander (1966)

Our practice must include getting to know the aspect within us that isn’t up against the test of time, soaking in it like a warm bath every chance we get; and yet in the same breath we must meet the challenge that this darkening human dream asks of us now. There is no escape from this great archetypal battle, whether we want it or not; all of us are being called on, our balance is being tested. All of us are being asked by the great force of life: When it comes to love and nourishing life, will you do what, in your heart, you know to be right?
योगस्थः कुरु कर्माणि सङ्गं त्यक्त्वा धनञ्जय।
सिद्ध्यसिद्ध्योः समो भूत्वा समत्वं योग उच्यते॥
yoga-sthaḥ kuru karmāṇi saṅgaṁ tyaktvā dhanañjaya |
siddhy-asiddhyoḥ samo bhūtvā samatvaṁ yoga uchyate ||
“Perform your duty established in yoga, abandoning attachment, O Arjuna, being indifferent to success and failure. This equanimity is called yoga.”
— Bhagavad Gītā 2.48
Tantralokā III.130
Devanāgarī
इत्थं प्रकाशातत्त्वस्य सोमसूर्याग्निताऽस्थितिः ।
अपि मुख्यम् तत्प्रकाशामात्रवत्त्वं न व्यपोह्यते ॥१३०॥
IAST
itthaṃ prakāśa-tattvasya soma-sūrya-agnitā sthitiḥ |
api mukhyam tat-prakāśa-mātratvaṃ na vyapohyate || 130 ||
Meaning
Consciousness appears as soma (nectar, soothing), sūrya (illumination), and agni (intensity, fire).
And yet its true nature as pure light (prakāśa-mātra) is never lost.

There is a verse I came across in the Tantralokā yesterday, and it struck me with its metaphorical depth and potency. It speaks of the three primary forms of light the ancients knew and that illuminated their lives: soma, sūrya, agni — moon, sun, and fire.

Its easy to muse on these wondrous lights: the rays of sun that catch heavy eyelids early in the morning; the billowing glow of a full autumn moon; the single candle at the center of an altar, bringing golden visages and deities to life. By these lights are revealed ten thousand textures and countless hues. Yet when all those varieties seem to speak of difference and divison, we must recall their singular essence. Like following the rays of color back through a prism, we find their source; one shade remains: pure light. This is the essential tantric insight.

We experience infinite varieties of consciousness - for every hue of color we can name, so too a mood: sweet sadness, mindless joy, mirthful anger, a spirited depression. These verbal designations fall infinitely short of consciousness’s true capacity. Yes, we can say “sweet sadness,” and maybe have some shared notion, but what is occurring now is this never-before-seen moment: the yellow of a leaf, the bark of a tree, a distant sound - the breaking of a twig, a wind that is cool but not unsettling.

To speak is to gesture toward experience, but speech alone can never match its infinite texture. In fact our linguistic and mental observations themselves are just another layer of texture, spices adding flavor, contributing to the never before tasted rasa of this moment. The wonder is how all these infinitely unique experiences are composed of one essence, the miracle of the one playing as the many.
The variegated mind reveals its innate qualities in phases, in lights:
the moon: the soothing calm after a hard day;
the sun: the clarity of knowing exactly what must be done;
the fire: the pulsing focus of emails, lunch, workouts, relations, difficult conversations.

And yet all these experience occur in the same eye, like these three lights harken back to the single source. In spiritual practice, these lights illuminate different steps on the path, different stages of the breath.
Moon — The Exhale, The Soothing Light

There is that moment of cool, nourishing calm when the weight of embodiment and responsibility begins to fall off. Through the meditative impulse to let go, we loosen the grip on everything that held us, tied as it were to the whipping post of our own ego’s expectations.

In that brief reprieve from the engineered obsession to do and be more, we may taste the nectar of simply being at peace with our own minds. This moon-light, this cooling softness, can be felt as the exhale, the easing out of effort and stress.
Sun — The Inhale, The Light of Realization

Then there is the sun: the realization that startles, rearranges, clarifies. When it rises, the shapes that once frightened us in the night reveal themselves in their true form. What we thought was a menacing figure, death over our shoulder, turns out to be a blossoming tree, a nourisher and protector grounding and guiding this life-force eternal.

This solar clarity allows us to see ourselves and our circumstances for what they are: a miracle. It shows us where we want to go and how to get there. And so we can associate this sunlight of understanding with the inhale — taking in the gift of a new breath, a new moment, a new day, a new life, full of wonder and possibility.
Fire — The Kumbhaka, The Transforming Flame

And finally, fire: the transformative flame. Sacred fire, stolen from the gods not only to guide the eyes but to transform whatever it touches. Fire brings out the essence of things, burns away impurities, and keeps alive the dream of warmth in all seasons.

In spiritual practice, this fire is indispensable, arising both by effort and grace. We may have inspiring insights and profound sighs of relief, but it is fire that harmonizes these forces and manifests them as our personified being. We sit in our own inner fire - the heat of austerity and devotion, the longing for merging, ecsatcy, and peace. Through the courage to stay in the flame, we alloy ourselves into something of richer caliber, while our confusions and collapses into ignorance naturally melt away.
This fire corresponds to the pause, the kumbhaka, the sitting down in the center, the abundant emptiness that transforms.
One Light, One Breath
And yet the teaching insists: all of these lights are truly one, prakāśa-mātra, pure light.
Just as all phases of the breath compose one breath, so too do the various lights of spiritual life compose one single process: awakening to the all-pervading, all-consuming radiance.
When we understand that every shade of experience expresses the universal Light, then we can allow ourselves to be illumined at every moment, regardless of emotional tone or energetic hue.
This is the never-ending story of self-realization:
the recognition that even your bones are made of nothing but Light.

title: While the devil is in the details, the divine is in the principle 𓇳

blocks.text: I write this at 2 a.m., unable to clear my mind of the cloudy impressions of an apparently darker time. Perhaps, as someone who has lived outside of the U.S. for a long time, I’m not qualified to write on domestic topics—maybe my finger is further from the pulse. Perhaps, given my profession as a yoga instructor, I might seem unqualified to espouse political philosophy and political science. Yet perhaps it is this distance that better allows me to see shapes on the horizon, like icebergs threatening imminent danger. As a student of yoga and psychology, I am familiar with the human mind’s ability to mislead itself, with the ego’s tendency to concretize illusions at every step, providing a sense of justification, security, and superiority. Perhaps a yogi is imagined as someone beyond the purview of preference and politics. But when it comes to an opportunity to help manifest wisdom and compassion, a person who claims to have character cannot ignore the invitation to act. This election, appearing monumental and posing questions of human goodnes, gives me the impetus to challenge the ways in which we might be seeing our situation.

Cognitive dissonance is one of the first concepts students learn in psychology. It’s the tension we experience when our beliefs, values, and actions don’t align, which eventually results in changing one of them to feel whole again. Think back to 2001: how many people truly believed the Iraqi government was involved in September 11th? But somehow the vast majority of voters and elected officials could do the cognitive gymnastics to equate any Middle Eastern Muslims to enemies. A persistent belief in fantastically destructive weapons was used as justification, until the awkward truth finally had to be shown, none could be found.

Today, cognitive dissonance might explain why we value some human lives more than others. This is perhaps the factor that lets us feel Israeli suffering is more real than Palestinian suffering, the factor that helps us believe a war in Europe is more tragic than a war in Sudan, the factor that enables us to see a migrant worker as less human than an American citizen. Through the mental gymnastics of seeing suffering but not speaking or acting against it, we solidify the illusion that someone is more worthy of goodness and life than somebody else. We are now living in this mass hallucination where some human lives are valued more than others; and until we collectively break out of this illusion, we will never truly be at peace.

And how is this week’s election any different? We are comfortably lining up to vote with our cognitive dissonance glasses on, unable to perceive the shades of cruelty, narcissism, incompetence, and malevolence right before our very eyes. And yet, if you don’t realize you are wearing these glasses, you might ask where any of these elements can be found. But would you be willing to take a step back from your deeply held views? Would you be willing to see an underlying unity amidst the diversity?

The realities we hide from when lost in our dissonance are as follows: threats of jailing political opponents (imagine being sent to jail for a piece like this), promises to deport millions of people who want to experience the same well-being that we all do (inevitably separating families and wreaking havoc on multinational stability), the clear and willful maneuvers to subvert the results of a presidential election (for the first time in American history), evidence of drives towards concentrated and total power, lack of concern about conflicts of interest (having elected leaders and their cronies making massive financial gains from public power), giving control of one of the world’s largest nuclear arsenals to someone who has shown themselves to be capricious and incompetent, giving control of the world’s largest economy to someone who is a climate change denier, along with a staggering list of racist, sexist, and other xenophobic claims. Because these facts are so inherently insidious, we find more and more fantastic justifications, as if by magic, to shield our eyes from them. This threat of an American demagogue is not one we can take lightly.

Demagoguery is no new phenomenon. From Caesar’s consolidation of Rome’s republic and coronation as dictator (his official title) to Nero’s voracious and vicious vanity, from Hitler’s to Stalin’s scapegoating of millions of people in their ideological brutality. Haven’t we seen this type of rhetoric and thinking repeat too often? It’s the same rhetoric that was being laughed at and cheered for last week in Madison Square Garden last week. Will we laugh and cheer if we become the cosigners of moral devastation and mass human suffering?

The French philosopher René Girard pointed out the persistent and pernicious human tendency to scapegoat. His work on mimetic theory suggests that human groups find unity by identifying a so-called “out-group” to blame for collective social and moral ills. Girard suggests that while this process might be initially unifying, it leads to cycles of violence and suffering. Perhaps we think we are too advanced and too rational to be caught by the same psychological forces. But this pride might be disastrous. Is that a risk worth taking? How many generations regret the suffering brought by their own delusional cycles of scapegoating? What would they implore us to see, to do today? Is it not clear that the same elements are coalescing now that led to tragedy prior? Alongside scapegoating, there is the consolidation of power, erosion of opposition, and the discrediting of vital institutions and scientific knowledge. Can you also appreciate these shapes on the horizon?

Reading this, dear friend, you might say, while I am aware of all those threats, I have good reason to neglect or disbelieve them. Perhaps you think: my vote is simply guided by potential personal gain, or as an act of rebellion against a system that props up one puppet politician after another, or the belief that all this talk is unnecessarily alarmist, or that I can’t agree with the details of her policies. Finally, you might say my vote is a necessary evil to attain a virtuous end. But where is the virtue in a world where you have a bigger slice of a rotting pie? With mass deportation, we’re discussing dissolving the vital roles played by millions of individuals. Will you pick the fruit in the fields? Will you quit your air-conditioned office job to build houses in the Arizona sun? Will you leave work early to care of your kid when there is a sudden shortage of childcare? And this doesn’t yet factor the human experience of so many individuals and families who we see so scapegoated at rally after rally.

You might not think Kamala Harris is qualified, you may think she is thrust undemocratically upon you, you might think the details of her platform are sparse. But while the devil is in the details, the divine is in the principle. This is a choice between a vision of unity versus one of division. If I may even wax emotional, it is a decision between love and fear, between kindness and hate. I am supporting Kamala Harris because it is a clear and obvious choice of someone who is earnestly speaking of unity. We as the people must drive her to that collective good, but unlike her alternative, she is someone who is not beyond reproach. Compare that to someone who is cynically beyond all criticism, who treats truth and the government like his plaything. The choice is abundantly clear.

In an ideal sense, government plays the role of protecting and fostering the growth of its people. But we, as people, must be wise enough to see beyond borders and passports to recognize that all people want the same things we do: health, happiness, and security. These are natural principles, genetically embedded and expressed by all conscious beings. When we honor these needs in others, we’re not just upholding their well-being; we’re reinforcing our own. True wisdom lies in shedding the illusion of separateness and recognizing that if we wish something for ourselves, we must support it for all.

In Buddhist teachings, this is called the realization of "emptiness" (śūnyatā), the understanding that all beings are interconnected, all of us are made of everything else. We’ve heard the myth of the self-made man for so long that our cognitive dissonance makes this teaching difficult to realize. But we can dissolve the painful illusion of a separate self by meditating on the truth that every breath we take, every sip of water we drink, every morsel of food we eat, even the language we think in, was not made by us. We are all the fluid manifestation of the same source, the vast universe of causes and conditions. We can also call this emptiness oneness. Sūnyatā-karuṇā-garbha: Oneness is the womb of compassion. From the view of interconnectedness, compassion (karuṇā) naturally arises, as one cannot truly harm others without ultimately harming oneself. Look at the truth of this operating in historical examples of cruelty that one group has inflicted upon another. Isn’t it the case that inevitably both groups suffer as one? If we’re brave enough to look at the survivors of war, we would see that the victors continue to suffer the pain of the vanquished. Emptiness shows us that we cannot escape the global environment that we collectively create. So now the question is: which kind of world do we want to live in?

This vision of emptiness isn’t simply some Buddhist nonsense; it’s clearly echoed in the teaching of Jesus. In John 13:34, he says, "A new commandment I give you: Love one another. As I have loved you, so you must love one another." How could we aspire to emulate that great teacher, if we are imbibing in venomous theories about people who don’t look like us or speak the same language as us? These words are here to break us out of the illusion that self and other are different, promoting acts that enshrine love rather than fear. Your vote is that act. How is it the case that a self-proclaimed Christian in America today is more likely to vote for someone who has such a disgraceful record of bigotry and misogyny? So, dear friend, if you vote, remember: this election is a referendum on our theory of life and humanity. The question is love or fear. And if you are not participating in this election, we are all still equally called, in our great acts and small, to create the world we want to experience by offering it to all.

title: Free Will and Cosmic Consciousness: Our Place in the Universe𓅊

blocks.text:
"By intense awareness and union with the pure essence of reality, one is freed from the limited individual powers."
 Śuddha-tattva-sandhānād vā apaśuśaktiḥ
 शुद्धतत्त्वसन्धानाद्वापशुशक्तिः
 (Śiva Sūtra 1.16)
vā = or
śuddha-tattva = the Pure Principle i.e. the Highest Śiva
sandhānād = by constant awareness
apaśuśaktiḥ = becomes like one in whom the binding power existing in the limited self is absent.
1. Are we Truly Free?

An ancient question continues to perplex philosophers, scientists, and spiritual seekers today: Do we really choose, are we truly free to decide, or are we merely acting out the script of some universal playwright, or our biology and the randomness of circumstance?  The idea that free will is an illusion is rooted in some of the most refined spiritual philosophies and is also aligned with a plethora of contemporary neuroscientific work. On the surface, this idea might seem quite menacing, almost nihilistic, that nothing I or others do is under our control and therefore we can harm and exploit without ever needing to assign responsibility. But what if, this realization, rather than a cause of despair, was a means for liberation? What if by realizing the deeply interpenetrating nature of all things, from neurons to cosmic consciousness, of essential oneness, served as the fundamental ground to live in greater harmony, compassion, and acceptance?

Recently I listened to Sam Harris interview Robert Sapolsky on his Making Sense podcast, and at first I was taken aback by their view that free will is an utter illusion. But it steadily dawned on me that this view acts as liberative understanding, rather than a constricting one. I will try my best to elucidate that point in a way that also serves to liberate you from an unnecessary and effectively illogical sense of shame.

In this exploration, we will plunge into perspectives of contemporary neuroscience, ancient wisdom from the Śiva Sūtra, and why the realization that we are not the sole authors of our lives is actually an invitation to live more blissfully.
2. Modern Debate Highlights the Ancient Illusion

Neuroscientist Robert Sapolsky and neuroscientist turned philosopher Sam Harris have both coherently argued the position that free will is an utter illusion. And this illusion can be seen through on both biologically and philosophical grounds. According to these writers, our thoughts and actions are shaped by innumerable forces outside of our control, each in turn shaped by other innumerable prior causes. For example, you didn’t choose the religion of your parents, the country you were born in, your sex, the color of your hair or eyes, the socioeconomic backdrop of your upbrining and the neurobiological propensity for the multiplicity of traits you experience as ‘me’ - like what food tastes best to you, how introverted or extroverted you feel, how many hours of sleep is optimal, etc. When we look at the sheer infinity of causes, which influence each other in incalculable ways, there is absolutely no place for an independent ‘self’ to exist who is free to choose. Buddhism 101 anyone?

Imagine a ripple in a pond. It has a certain shape and speed, we could call this its character. Now the ripple doesn’t decide it’s character; rather it’s caused by a stone dropped into the water. Similarly, our selves and behaviors are ripples interacting in a cosmic pond of causality. Each neuron firing, each thought we have, is the result of previous causes, all beyond our personal control, all linked to the infinity of action which has come before. We may feel as though agency, but this is a byproduct of the intricate web of causes and effects. Harris uses the metaphor of wetness and a water molecule. A water molecule in and of itself doesn’t have the property of wetness, rather wetness is an emergent property of millions of water molecules coalescing. So to does a single neuron not contain agency, it simply fires or doesn’t, but across billions of neurons coalescing the feeling of being free to choose emerges, but can this ghost actually be found in the machine?

Modern research suggests most clearly, no. Benjamin Libet’s 1983 experiment still serves as the standard today. Libet found that the brain prepares for an action before we're even aware of deciding to move, suggesting that our sense of conscious control may follow our brain’s decisions rather than leading them. John-Dylan Haynes followed up on Libet’s work in 2008 by using fMRI technology. He demonstrated that scientists could predict participants' choices up to seven seconds before they consciously made the decision, showing that unconscious brain activity precedes conscious decision-making by a significant margin. Further work went on to show that the brain perhaps demonstrates some ability to veto one of these ‘unconscious’ decisions, perhaps offering some form of “free-wont”.  But in Harris’s and Sapolsky’s view that entire veto process would also be based on the inescapable influence of our unchosen psychobiology and lived experience. Due to these reasonings and findings many neuroscientists now hold that our sense of making conscious decisions is just an illusion.
3. Our Intuitions and Counterarguments

There is, of course, a debate from other formidable thinkers on this point. Take Daniel Dennet for example, he suggests a contemporary form of compatibilism, where both free will and determinism exist simultaneously. He reasons in his work Freedom Evolves (2003), as most of us our likely to do, that we can still consider ourselves to be “free” if through rational deliberation and reflection we can align our actions with our deeply held desires and intentions. At first glance, we like this seemingly more nuanced approach, as it serves as the basis for our entire human sphere full of moral agency and possibility. It allows us to justify both reward and punishment to persons who we consider the author of their good and bad acts. Taken to its furthest extent this is the philosophy of the saved and the damned, those who deserve suffering or happiness because of their free choices.

Yet this view has deep logical inconsistencies. Aligning our actions to our desires and intentions might be more coherent, perhaps even resulting in happiness, but those desires and intentions are not our own. Every desire we have today is shaped by biological or social forces, I might desire a wonderful life, however I define it, but certainly that definition is based on biological and psychological needs which are clearly outside of my choosing. If we are brave enough to stretch our minds to the point, we can touch the truth that all of this was beyond any personal choosing. And rather than being depressing, this is a cause for liberation.
4. True Freedom and Where to Find It

Perhaps today’s materialist science leaves us with a cold stark feeling of determinism. But centuries prior texts like the Śiva Sūtra explored the nature of reality and the self, showing that while an individual being or jīva, is bound by cirumstance, the true self remains absolutely free.
In Śiva Sūtra 1.16, we find this profound teaching:

Śuddha-tattva-sandhānād vā apaśuśaktiḥ
 शुद्धतत्त्वसन्धानाद्वापशुशक्तिः
 "Or by constant awareness of the Pure Priniciple, he becomes like one in whom the binding power existing in the limited self is absent." -Trans. Jaideva Singh

The verse points to the illusion of individuality: our sense of being separate entities, literally here as animals or paśu, with our own sense of power, śakti. In the non-dual Śiva Tantra freedom belongs not to the apparent individual but to the Universal Consciousness itself. It is this śuddha-tattva, the Pure Principle, that is both the original cause and the all-pervasive substance. It is both the rock thrown in the water and the interacting dance of ripples. When we recognize the śuddha-tattva as everything we observe, from our cells to the sunset, we transcend then illusion of being a self-determined and individual being, and realize ourselves to be what we truly are: the comic essence itself.

Just as modern science shows that our decisions are shaped by biological process, so to do the Śiva Sūtras that all our thoughts and actions are the direct expressions of universal consciousness. There is no room for real separate agents, only one unified essence, experiencing itself in and through its infinite modifications.

In fact, the highest principle in this non-dual Śiva Tantra is free-will, or svātantrya. This is not the free-will of some limited or contracted ‘I’, rather this is the cosmic freedom that is the force that put the infinitude of causes in motion, that is the cause that led you to be reading these very words right now. We attain true freedom not through by determining our desires and decisions, but by realizing that we are identical to the force that determined and desired all of this.  At the absolute level, we are one with the free, creative consciousness that is the source of all.
5. Liberation from Guilt and Blame

At first, the idea that we don’t have free will may feel unsettling. If we aren’t in control, then what’s the point? Why bother trying to be good or striving to achieve anything? The answer lies in a profound shift in perspective—one that is the dawning of an authentic spiritual life.

Freedom from Guilt and Shame: If our thoughts and actions are determined by forces beyond our control, we can begin to let go of the heavy burden of guilt, shame, and inadequacy. No longer do we need to judge ourselves harshly for not being “good enough” or making mistakes. We are simply expressions of the universe, unfolding according to its laws. The teaching of apaśuśaktiḥ (freedom from limited powers) encourages us to throw off the burden of constant self-condemnation.

Self-Acceptance: Contemporary philosophy and the Śiva Sūtras teach us that there is nothing inherently flawed about what we do and how we think. Every success, every failure, every idiosyncrasy is an expression of the infinite web of causes and effects. This is Indra’s Net, we live in a holographic universe where everything contains traces of everything else. Nothing is independent of anything else. We are perfect manifestations of Nature or the pure essence of reality. Recognizing this frees us from the toxic need for perfectionism.

Compassion for Others: Understanding that others, too, are the product of circumstances beyond their control fosters deeper compassion. When someone acts out of anger, fear, or confusion, we can recognize that they are not choosing those actions in a vacuum—they are expressions of a vast network of causes. Just as we seek to be understood, we can extend that same understanding to others, breaking down the walls of judgment.
6. Moving with Nature Instead of Against It

Accepting that the ego has not real freedom is freedom, freedom from the illusion of control. Life is not something we need to battle or control, but something we can flow with. Like the ripple in the pond, we are the motion of the universe. The Śiva Sūtra reminds us that when we recall our pure essence, śuddha tattva, we transcend the illusion of separateness and realize that we are part of the cosmic dance.

In a practical sense, this means letting go of the constant need to "fix" ourselves, others, and the world around us. We can still strive for positive change, that is of course natural intelligence, in fact it is Nature’s Intelligence, moving though us in every cell of our being. Great peace can be felt and wisdom implemented in trusting the intelligence moving through us rather than making it a limited personal possession to be proud or ashamed of.
7. Practical Implementation: How to Live with This Understanding
How might it be helpful to apply this refined position of freedom to our lives? Here are a few possibilities:

Let Go of Perfectionism: Realizing that you are not the sole author of your actions releases the pressure to always get things right. You are already and always enough as you are—a pure expression of Nature or Śuddha Tattva.

Cultivate Compassion: When you understand that everyone, including yourself, is a product of causes beyond control, you naturally develop more empathy for yourself and others. You are free to forgive more easily and hold less resentment. We can advocate for systems of justice that champion rehabilitation and restraint rather than punishment and harm.

Celebrate Your Place in the Universe: Rather than feeling like a small, isolated being, reframe your existence as a wave in the ocean or a jewel in Indra’s Net. Every thought, action, and experience is part of a great interconnected process, you reflect everything else, and everything else reflects you. See the beauty that you are the universal expressed in dynamic, infinite uniqueness.
8. Conclusion: The Beauty of Being a Cosmic Manifestation

In both the scientific and spiritual logic, we find a profound message: we are not isolated beings, struggling for control in a chaotic world. Instead, we are part of a larger, interconnected flow—whether you call it the laws of nature or Śuddha Tattva. This recognition frees us from guilt, blame, and the burden of regret.

For the sanity of our human world we must overcome the invasive intuition that we are somehow flawed or broken; we are immediate manifestations of the universe, ripples in the cosmic water. The realization that we have no free will as assumed in not one of dread, but of beauty—we are all expressions of the one infinite intelligence, and in that, we find our real freedom.
